e: 'Many a + singular noun' construction — 'an hour' fits with 'many' omitted for this test; correct fixed phrase is 'many an hour'.

t: Identify the sentence that correctly uses the indefinite article.
o: I have an uniform in my wardrobe
I have never seen an UFO in an English movie
I have never seen a UFO in an English movie
I have never seen a UFO in a English movie
e: "UFO" को "yoo" sound से pronounce किया जाता है जो consonant sound है, इसलिए "a UFO" सही है। "English" vowel sound से शुरू होता है इसलिए "an English" सही है।

t: Identify the sentence that correctly uses the indefinite article.
o: She is a Indian artist married to an European engineer.
She is an Indian artist married to an European engineer.
She is an Indian artist married to a European engineer.
She is a Indian artist married to a European engineer
e: 'C). She is an Indian artist married to a European engineer.' का चयन होगा क्योंकि असंख्यक अनुच्छेद का सही प्रयोग यहाँ पर हुआ है। "Indian" शब्द जो कि स्वर से आरंभ होता है, के पहले 'an' का प्रयोग होता है। वही, "European" शब्द जो कि 'y' ध्वनि से आरंभ होता है, के पहले 'a' का प्रयोग होता है। इसलिए, 'C' विकल्प सही है।

t: Identify the sentence that correctly uses the indefinite article.
o: She is a MBA graduate with a honorary doctorate.
She is an MBA graduate with an honorary doctorate.
She is a MBA graduate with an honorary doctorate.
She is an MBA graduate with a honorary doctorate.
e: Only the sentence in option (b) has the correct use of indefinite articles. The article 'an' is used before words that start with a vowel or a vowel-sounding word. Accordingly, 'MBA' and 'honorary' start with a vowel sound. So, the use of 'an' is correctly used in option (b). Hence, the correct answer is option (b). Note: Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t: Identify the sentence that correctly uses the indefinite article.

She suggested a elaborate approach but mine is a easier one.
She suggested an elaborate approach but mine is an easier one.
e: Note: Only the sentence in option (d) has the correct use of indefinite articles. The article 'an' is used before words that start with a vowel or a vowel sounding word. Accordingly, 'elaborate' and 'easier' start with a vowel. So, the use of 'an' is correctly used in option (d). Hence, the correct answer is option (d). Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

t: Select the option with the correct use of article(s).
o: I was rude to him when I was in an fit of rage.
I was rude to him when I was in fit of rage.
I was rude to him when I was in the fit of rage.
I was rude to him when I was in a fit of rage.
e:
· "an fit of rage" (Option 1) is incorrect because "fit" starts with a consonant sound, so "an" cannot be used.
· "in fit of rage" (Option 2) is incorrect because an article is required before "fit."
· "in the fit of rage" (Option 3) is grammatically possible but not commonly used.
· "in a fit of rage" (Option 4) is correct because "a" is used before singular countable nouns when referring to an unspecified instance.

t: Select the option with the correct use of article(s).
o: She kept lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
She kept an lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
She kept a lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
She kept the lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
e: The expression "a lot of" is the correct form that means "many" or "much." "Lot of" without an article is grammatically incorrect. "An lot" is incorrect because we use "an" before words beginning with vowel sounds, and "lot" begins with a consonant sound. "The lot of" would be used only in specific contexts where a particular lot is being referenced, which isn't the case here.
